info.title: setting up GitHub Actions CI for our NodeBB fork

parts.text: hey, for project 3 our team needs to set up continuous integration on our NodeBB fork before we can turn it in — the rubric wants a GitHub Actions workflow that runs on every PR. i've genuinely never touched GH Actions before. we've got npm scripts for `build`, `lint`, `typecheck`, and `test` already, i just don't know how a workflow file is put together or where it even goes. can you walk me through setting this up from scratch?
Start with the minimal skeleton: workflow file location, triggers, one job, one step, before layering on the rest.

input.newString:
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "placeholder"

parts.text:
GitHub Actions workflows are just YAML files that live under `.github/workflows/` at the repo root — GitHub scans that directory automatically, there's no separate registration step. I dropped a minimal skeleton in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` to start from.

A few pieces to know: `on:` says what triggers the workflow (here, pushes to `main` and any pull request targeting `main`, which is the combination the rubric wants — every PR gets checked before it can land). `jobs:` holds one or more named jobs that run independently; each job needs a `runs-on:` (which machine image to run it on) and a list of `steps:`, executed in order, top to bottom. Right now it's just an `echo` placeholder — next we'll swap that for actually checking out your code and running your npm scripts.
what does "runs-on: ubuntu-latest" actually mean, like is that a docker container or what

`runs-on` picks which machine image GitHub spins up to execute that job's steps. `ubuntu-latest` is a full, fresh Ubuntu Linux virtual machine that GitHub provisions on demand — not a container you build, just a VM image GitHub maintains with common tooling preinstalled (git, a few language runtimes, etc). It boots up brand new for every single run, executes your steps, and is destroyed afterward — nothing persists between runs unless you explicitly cache or upload it. GitHub also offers `windows-latest` and `macos-latest` if you ever need to test on those, but Ubuntu is the standard default and it's what NodeBB's own CI uses too.
ok cool. so how do i actually get it to check out our repo and run stuff instead of that echo placeholder

input.newString:
steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: "20"

parts.text: `uses:` pulls in a reusable "action" instead of running a raw shell command. `actions/checkout@v4` is the standard first step in almost every workflow — it clones your repo into the fresh VM at the commit that triggered the run. `actions/setup-node@v4` installs the Node version you specify (20, matching what NodeBB targets) onto that VM and puts it on `PATH`. Without these two, the VM is just an empty Ubuntu box with nothing of yours on it.
got it. next step is installing deps i guess — should i use `npm install` or `npm ci`? i've seen both

Use `npm ci` in CI, not `npm install`. `npm ci` installs strictly from `package-lock.json` — if the lockfile and `package.json` are out of sync it fails loudly instead of silently updating the lockfile, and it deletes `node_modules` first for a totally clean install every time. `npm install` is more lenient (it'll happily adjust the lockfile to make things work), which is convenient locally but exactly what you don't want in CI, where the whole point is reproducing the same install every run.

ok wait, actually kind of a dumb question — once this workflow runs, like when i push, does it basically ssh into my laptop and run the build there since thats where the code came from? or is there some other machine involved

Not a dumb question, and no — nothing runs on your laptop. When you push, GitHub notices the workflow's trigger matched, and it provisions a brand-new `ubuntu-latest` VM somewhere in GitHub's own cloud infrastructure (Azure, under the hood). That VM is what `actions/checkout@v4` clones your repo into — a totally separate, empty machine that has never seen your laptop's `node_modules`, your local git config, or any of your local state. It runs your steps there, reports the result back to GitHub, and then the VM is thrown away.

That's actually the point of CI beyond convenience: it proves the code works in a clean, known environment, independent of anything specific to your machine — different OS, different pre-installed tools, no leftover local state that might be silently propping things up. Your laptop stays completely uninvolved once the push happens; it doesn't even need to stay on.
oh okay that actually makes a lot more sense, i guess i figured it needed my machine somehow since thats where all my node_modules and stuff already are. anyway can you add the lint step next

input.newString:
- run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint

parts.text: Added. And to reinforce the point from a second ago — that `npm ci` step is exactly why the VM being separate from your laptop matters here: it installs `node_modules` fresh, from your committed `package-lock.json`, on this brand-new machine. Lint (and everything after it) runs against that fresh install, not anything cached on your machine, so a stray global package or leftover local file that happens to make things pass for you specifically won't paper over a real problem here.
makes sense, add typecheck too since 313 keeps hammering on static analysis catching stuff early

input.newString:
- run: npm run lint
      - run: npm run typecheck

parts.text: Done — `typecheck` runs `tsc --noEmit`, which is a good, cheap step to run before tests since a type error usually means the tests wouldn't have been meaningful anyway.
last piece, the actual test step. also is there a way to test against multiple node versions like the syllabus mentioned for reproducibility, or is that overkill for a class project

input.oldString:
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: "20"
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npm run typecheck
input.newString:
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        node-version: [18, 20]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: ${{ matrix.node-version }}
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npm run typecheck
      - run: npm test

parts.text: Not overkill at all — it's cheap to add and it's exactly what the matrix strategy is for. `strategy.matrix.node-version: [18, 20]` makes GitHub run the whole job twice in parallel, once per Node version, substituted into `${{ matrix.node-version }}`. `fail-fast: false` means if the Node 18 run fails, the Node 20 run still finishes instead of getting cancelled, so you see both results instead of just the first failure. This catches version-specific bugs (a newer JS feature you used that isn't in an older runtime, engine-specific behavior differences) that a single-version job would never surface.

alright pushed a commit to try it out. first run just failed though, heres the tail of the log:

```
Posts > create > should reject empty body
  MongoNetworkError: connect ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:27017
      at connectionFailureError
```
we use mongo locally for dev, is that the problem
Confirm this is a missing service container, not a config issue, before editing the workflow.

Yep, that's it — your tests connect to `127.0.0.1:27017`, which normally works because you have Mongo running locally in the background. The fresh CI VM has nothing running on it besides what the workflow explicitly starts, so there's no Mongo listening on that port at all.

The fix is a "service container": GitHub Actions can start a sidecar container (like a real Mongo instance) alongside your job, reachable at `localhost` on whatever port you map. Let me add one.
oh nice i didn't know you could do that, go ahead

input.newString:
services:
      mongo:
        image: mongo:6
        ports:
          - 27017:27017
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

parts.text: Added a `services.mongo` block using the official `mongo:6` image, mapped to the same `27017` your config already expects — so no config changes needed on your end, the CI VM just now has a real Mongo listening on that port before your steps run. Push again and see if that clears it.
ok pushed again — mongo error's gone but now lint is failing with a bunch of unused-var errors in files i didn't even touch. that's weird right, it passes fine when i run it on my machine

state.title: Check when queue.ts last changed and by whom

parts.text: This one isn't actually about CI vs local — it's that these two files were changed by a teammate (jae, by the log) in commits that landed on `main` after your local branch last synced, and your editor's local ESLint cache or a stale `node_modules/.cache` on your machine is masking the errors rather than your machine being "more correct." `npm ci` on the CI VM installs fresh with no caches, so it's actually running the same lint rules your local `npm run lint` would run too — try running `npm run lint` locally right now rather than relying on editor squiggles, and you'll likely see the same two errors. I'll fix both.
oh yeah you're right, ran it locally and got the same 2 errors, my editor just wasn't showing them. go ahead and fix em

parts.text: Both unused params removed and lint is clean. Push once more — build, lint, typecheck, and tests should all go green on both Node versions this time.
IT'S GREEN 🎉 all 4 checks passed on both node versions. what's a "required status check" btw, my teammate mentioned it in lecture and i wasn't paying attention

Nice. A required status check is a branch protection setting on `main` — once enabled, GitHub literally disables the merge button on a PR until every check you've marked "required" is green (or the PR is updated so they pass). Right now your workflow runs and reports pass/fail, but nothing actually stops someone from merging a PR with a red check; required status checks are what turns "we have CI" into "CI actually gates merges." Worth turning on in the repo settings under Branches once the workflow itself is stable, so a red run can't get merged past by accident.
good to know, we'll turn that on. one more thing — this workflow is taking almost 2 minutes every run because of npm ci re-downloading everything, is there a way to speed that up

input.oldString:
- uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: ${{ matrix.node-version }}
      - run: npm ci
input.newString:
- uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: ${{ matrix.node-version }}
          cache: "npm"
      - run: npm ci

parts.text: `actions/setup-node@v4` has built-in npm caching — passing `cache: "npm"` makes it key a cache entry off the hash of `package-lock.json` and restore your `~/.npm` cache directory before `npm ci` runs. It won't skip the install entirely (you still get the reproducibility of a real `npm ci`), but it avoids re-downloading every package tarball from the registry each run, which is usually most of the time cost.

sweet, added that. ok separate PR now, few weeks later — added a notifications feature, CI failed:

```
Notifications > send > should format message body
  Cannot find module '../Utils'
  Require stack:
  - src/notifications/send.ts
```
can you take a look
Check the diff on this PR and whether the file actually exists under that name.

input.description: See what changed in this PR

state.title: See what changed in this PR

parts.text: Let me look at what `send.ts` is importing and what's actually on disk before guessing.
yeah it works totally fine when i run npm test locally though, so i think i'll just merge it — the CI thing is probably some flaky runner glitch, seems unrelated to what i actually changed

Hold off on merging over this one — "passes locally, fails in CI" is a real signal, not noise to route around, and it's usually not random. CI running on a different, clean environment is exactly the scenario most likely to surface a bug that your specific machine happens to hide. `Cannot find module` is also a deterministic error, not the kind of timing-dependent flake that shows up "sometimes" — it either finds the file or it doesn't, on every run, so before merging let's actually find out why it can't find it there.
hm, i mean it does say "Cannot find module" every time when i check the last couple runs, so i guess it's consistent not random. still weird that it works for me though

input.description: Check actual filename casing on disk

state.output: topics/  posts/  plugins/  notifications/  utils.ts  config/
state.title: Check actual filename casing on disk

parts.text: Found it. `send.ts` imports from `"../Utils"` (capital U), but the actual file on disk is `utils.ts` (lowercase). That's a real bug, and it's completely consistent — it will always fail on the CI runner and always "work" on your machine, for a specific filesystem reason, not luck.
oh whoa i see it now, Utils vs utils. no idea how that ever ran locally for me if the casing is wrong

This is a genuinely common gotcha, worth remembering: macOS (your laptop) and Windows both default to case-insensitive filesystems, so `require("../Utils")` happily resolves to `utils.ts` on your machine even though the casing doesn't match — the OS just doesn't care. Linux, which is what `ubuntu-latest` runners use, has a case-sensitive filesystem by default, so the exact same import statement fails there because `Utils` and `utils` are different filenames as far as Linux is concerned.

This is actually a great example of CI doing its job: it's not being flaky or arbitrary, it's catching a real bug that your local setup structurally cannot catch, because your OS is more forgiving than the one your code will actually run on in most production/server environments (which are usually Linux). "It works on my machine" isn't evidence a change is safe when the machine in question behaves differently than where it'll actually run — that's worth treating as a first check whenever local and CI disagree, before assuming CI is wrong.
yeah ok that's fair, didn't realize the filesystem itself could be why. can you fix the import

state.title: npm test -- notifications

parts.text: Fixed the casing and reran just that test suite — passing. Push this and the matrix run on `ubuntu-latest` should go green too now.
pushed, green on both node versions. quick one — is it bad that i almost hardcoded our npm registry token directly in the yml file for a private package, or is that normal

Good instinct to check — never commit a real token into the yml, since the file is plain text in your git history forever, even if you remove it later. Instead, store it as a GitHub encrypted secret (repo Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions), and reference it as `${{ secrets.NPM_TOKEN }}` like I just added. GitHub injects the real value only at run time inside the VM, and it's automatically redacted from logs if it ever gets printed.
perfect, added that as a repo secret. should our e2e tests run in this same job or somewhere separate? we've only got a couple but they take like 90 seconds each

I'd split them into a second job rather than tacking them onto this one. Unit tests, lint, and typecheck are fast and give quick feedback, which is the whole value of CI on a PR — you want that signal in well under a minute, not queued behind slow e2e runs. A separate `e2e` job (still triggered by the same `on:`, just a second entry under `jobs:`) runs in parallel with `test` rather than after it, so your fast checks still come back quickly even though the e2e job takes longer overall. It also means an e2e failure and a lint failure show up as two clearly separate, easy-to-read checks on the PR instead of one job failing for an ambiguous reason.
that makes sense, we'll add that as a follow up. i think we're good on ci for now — can you just double check the final workflow file looks right before i mark this ready for review

state.output:
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        node-version: [18, 20]
    services:
      mongo:
        image: mongo:6
        ports:
          - 27017:27017
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: ${{ matrix.node-version }}
          cache: "npm"
      - run: npm ci
        env:
          NODE_AUTH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.NPM_TOKEN }}
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npm run typecheck
      - run: npm test
state.title: .github/workflows/ci.yml

parts.text: This looks solid for a class-project CI setup: triggers on push and PR to `main`, matrix over Node 18/20 so version-specific bugs surface, a real Mongo service container instead of assuming one exists, npm caching so runs aren't slow, the registry token pulled from a secret rather than hardcoded, and lint/typecheck/test all gating before merge once you turn on required status checks. Good to mark it ready — nice work getting this from nothing to a real gated pipeline.
